Client work doesn't wait for a sprint

If you run a small agency or freelance studio, you know the real bottleneck isn't ideas — it's dev hours. A client wants to "see something" before they'll sign off on a project. A campaign needs a landing page by Friday, not by the next sprint. And every hour a developer spends building a throwaway mockup is an hour not spent on billable, committed work.

Most AI website builders solve this by handing you a templated site that looks fine in a demo and falls apart the moment a client asks for a real change. Kodely takes a different approach: you describe the site in plain English, and it generates an actual Vite + React 19 + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS v4 codebase — real components, not a page builder wrapped around a template.

Where Kodely fits into an agency workflow

Kodely is built for the fast, iterative front end of client work — the part before a project justifies a dedicated dev sprint:

  • Describe it, get a working app. Type what the site should be, and Kodely builds it from a real foundation of hand-built UI primitives, not a locked template.
  • Watch it compile live. The live preview renders the actual app as it's generated, so you and the client are looking at the real thing, not a static mock.
  • Publish in one click. Every project gets a free public URL at <name>.kodely.site — no hosting setup, no deploy step.
  • Keep iterating in chat. Client wants the hero copy changed, a section reordered, a new page added? Describe the change and Kodely edits the real components. Checkpoints let you roll back to any prior version for free if a change goes sideways.
  • See the code. The generated source is viewable and copyable right in the app, so a developer can pick up the real component code once a project is worth building out further.

Be clear-eyed about what this covers today: Kodely generates front-end apps only. There's no backend, database, auth, or payment generation, no custom domain connection, and no project export or zip download — you view and copy code in-app. Editing is chat-driven, not click-to-edit, and there's no team or multi-seat collaboration layer yet. For the specific job of getting a real, visually convincing site in front of a client fast, none of that is usually what's blocking you at the prototype stage.

Three ways agencies actually use Kodely

1. Pitch prototypes before you commit dev time

Instead of a slide deck or a static Figma mock, build a working site for the pitch. Prospective clients can click through an actual app in the browser, on their own phone, before you've written a single line of production code. If the pitch doesn't land, you've spent credits, not a developer's afternoon.

2. Quick landing pages for client campaigns

A client launching a promotion or event often needs a dedicated landing page fast, with a short shelf life. Describe the campaign, the offer, and the look, publish it to a kodely.site URL, and it's live. It's a good fit for pages that need to exist quickly and don't need a custom domain or backend logic.

3. Throwaway concepts for internal review

Before an account lead brings a direction to a client, it helps to see it as a real, navigable site rather than a mockup — different layouts, different tones, different structures. Kodely makes it cheap to generate two or three real variants, compare them live, and throw away the ones that don't work, without touching your team's actual dev capacity.

Pricing: honest answer, no agency tier yet

There's no separate agency plan on Kodely today, and we're not going to pretend otherwise. Every account — solo freelancer, in-house team, or agency — runs on the same pricing:

  • Free to start: 750 credits on signup, no card required.
  • $9 for 500 credits
  • $40 for 2,500 credits (most popular)
  • $90 for 6,000 credits

Credits are metered from actual AI cost, and a build that fails to compile is never charged. For agencies, that means you can run several client prototypes on the free tier before spending anything, and top up as real projects come in. See the full breakdown on the pricing page.
